channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: Arizona teen builds website to help families find dual-language schools
item.description: Arizona Luminaria: “Meaning ‘navigator’ in English, the site supports families with questions about dual-language programs and details the model used. Its features include a school finder based on zip codes, state letter grades and shows whether buses are available to and from school.”

item.title: FBI started buying Americans’ location data again, Kash Patel confirms
item.description: Ars Technica: “Three years after saying it had stopped buying location data of Americans without a warrant, the FBI acknowledged it has restarted the purchases. During questioning at a Senate Select Committee on Intelligence hearing yesterday, FBI Director Kash Patel said the location data purchases have produced valuable information, and he did not commit to stopping the practice.”

item.title: UK police force presses pause on live facial recognition after study finds racial bias
item.description: The Register: “A UK police force has suspended its deployment of live facial recognition (LFR) technology after a study revealed it was statistically more likely to identify Black people on a watchlist database.”

item.title: The Cannes Film Festival is buying into the creator economy in a big way
item.description: Tubefilter: “The 2026 edition of the venerable film festival will put an unprecedented amount of focus on creators and their work. On May 17, the Cannes marketplace — known in French as the Marché du Film — will host an event that will gather some of the creator economy’s foremost leaders, influencers, and innovators.”

item.title: Citing suicides, Minnesota lawmakers want to end minors’ access to AI companions
item.description: Eden Prairie Local News: “A 13-year-old in Colorado, a 14-year-old in Florida and a 16-year-old in California: all three of them died by suicide since 2023 after prolonged and troubling conversations with artificial intelligence chatbots. Now in Minnesota, lawmakers are considering whether to make companion-style AI illegal for people under age 18. If passed, the law would be the first of its kind in the U.S. amid a wake of legislation aimed at regulating the industry.”

item.title: Luke Littler applies to trademark his face to combat AI fakes
item.description: BBC: “Luke Littler, the youngest darts world champion in history, has applied to the Intellectual Property Office to trademark his face. The move is intended to prevent his face being reproduced, including by generative AI, without permission.”

item.title: Greater Than Zero: The Anti-AI Pushback On Gaming Preservation Efforts Makes No Sense
item.description: Techdirt: “I’m not some AI evangelist. I fully recognize that there are error and other problems with AI… and I imagine there always will be, to some extent. AI is not always, or perhaps even mostly, the right tool to use. Nor will it always have benefits that outweigh problems it creates for we human beings. But a positive number is greater than zero. This was a tool that suddenly made all of this culture content accessible to a wider range of people.”

item.title: AI is running rampant in health care. They want to fix that.
item.description: Northeastern University: “AI has been widely adopted in health care systems nationwide, but there is still no central framework for how to do so ethically. By creating a universal guidebook, researchers at Northeastern hope to fill that gap.”

item.title: The Old Internet is Still Here
item.description: Tyler Gaw: “We’re still making stuff we care about and sharing that stuff on our websites. We’re making it for ourselves first, but we’re also making it for you. This Good Internet Stuff may take effort to find. You probably won’t see it in a feed. It will not have likes and RTs. It might be months old by the time you see it. But, it’ll be here. Waiting.”

item.title: Full circle: Researchers turn food waste into energy, use the process water to grow food
item.description: McMaster University: “Researchers from the faculties of Engineering and Science are teaming up to convert agricultural food waste into energy-dense solid fuel, then use the water left over from the process as an eco-friendly pesticide and fertilizer.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Chasing the Superbloom: New Map Helps Campers Time Wildflower Trips
item.description: Santa Barbara Independent: “The California Superbloom Forecast pulls from roughly five years of research-grade observations submitted through the community science platform iNaturalist. By analyzing more than 150,000 entries, Hipcamp’s team created a map intended to guide visitors toward bloom-rich areas while also encouraging responsible recreation.”

item.title: Digital Window Opens Onto UNE’s Collections
item.description: University of New England (Australia): “UNE has launched its Collections Gateway, a digital portal providing access to carefully curated historical, cultural, and academic material amassed in the University’s unique collections over decades.”

item.title: Microsoft Is Finally Ready to Make Windows 11 Less Terrible After Bloating It With AI Crap
item.description: Gizmodo: “According to a blog post from Pavan Davuluri, EVP of Windows & Devices at Microsoft, updates will roll out to Windows Insiders starting next month and target a few key areas, though most of them have to do with making the overall experience less frustrating.”

item.title: Roblox’s 18+ usership is growing 50% year over year
item.description: Tubefilter: “KreekCraft is one of the biggest Roblox YouTubers out there–but when he unveiled his own game development studio last month, he said his motivation for launching it was because there aren’t many games that appeal to him as a nearly 30-year-old adult.”

item.title: Google Business Profile tests AI-generated replies to reviews
item.description: Search Engine Land: What could possibly go wrong. “Google is testing AI-generated review replies in Google Business Profile…. Responding to reviews can impact conversions and trust. But generic AI replies could be risky and erode trust, especially on negative reviews where authenticity matters most. Response quality matters more than whether a business replies to reviews.”

item.title: Nevada utility to Lake Tahoe: Find electricity elsewhere
item.description: CalMatters: “Lake Tahoe’s longtime power supplier, NV Energy, will cut off the region next year. It has said data centers are driving ‘unprecedented’ demand.”

item.title: New Swiss foundation to catalogue Jean-Luc Godard’s film archive
item.description: SwissInfo: “The Jean-Luc Godard Foundation has ambitious goals: to list, preserve and share Godard’s archive. The French-Swiss film director died in 2022, leaving behind works scattered worldwide and the thorny matter of film rights.”

item.title: This Massive Data Breach Leaked 2.7 Million Social Security Numbers
item.description: Lifehacker: “Another massive data breach has compromised millions of Americans’ healthcare data and sensitive information. Navia Benefit Solutions, a benefits administrator for more than 10,000 U.S. employers, has disclosed a hack that affects nearly 2.7 million individuals, according to a March 18 filing with the Maine Attorney General.”

item.title: Man known as ‘K$’ used Facebook to scam hundreds of thousands from investors
item.description: NJ.com: “A previously suspended investment broker has admitted to defrauding investors of hundreds of thousands of dollars in a social media scam. Kenneth Thom, 42, of Westfield, pleaded guilty to investment adviser fraud in Manhattan federal court on Thursday, the U.S. Attorney’s Office Southern District of New York said in a statement.”

item.title: Using your AI chatbot as a search engine? Be careful what you believe
item.description: The Conversation: “Search engines rely on articles and text about a given topic, and then weigh how reliable those articles are. Generative AI instead relies on huge bodies of text, from which it measures the odds of words appearing next to each other. These ‘large language models’ are purely looking to generate reasonable-looking sentences, rather than accurate ones.”

item.title: News chatbots that present multiple viewpoints tend to earn the trust of conspiracy believers
item.description: PsyPost: “The research provides evidence that individuals who hold strong conspiracy beliefs tend to respond well to these chatbots, viewing them as useful tools for reading diverse news. These findings point to new ways technology might help pierce information bubbles and reduce societal division by exposing people to multiple perspectives.”

item.title: New computer chip material inspired by the human brain could slash AI energy use
item.description: University of Cambridge: “Researchers have developed a new kind of nanoelectronic device that could dramatically cut the energy consumed by artificial intelligence hardware by mimicking the human brain. The researchers, led by the University of Cambridge, developed a form of hafnium oxide that acts as a highly stable, low‑energy ‘memristor’ — a component designed to mimic the efficient way neurons are connected in the brain.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Music manuscripts from Cologne now linked to digitized copies
item.description: Répertoire International des Sources Musicales: “A while ago the Cologne University and City Library (RISM siglum D-KNu) provided us with a list of links to newly digitized copies, which we have promptly added to the corresponding RISM records. The collection had been cataloged for RISM in 2014; the current update significantly enhances the usability of these source descriptions by adding links to no fewer than 480 of them.”

item.title: Live from GDC… 1989! 21 hours of vintage talks from early gaming luminaries
item.description: Video Game History Foundation: “Last week was GDC 2026, but we’re not done with GDC just yet. Today, we’re opening a new collection of talk recordings from the 1989 Computer Game Developers’ Conference!”

item.title: State updates pollution mapping tool to identify communities most at risk
item.description: Los Angeles Wave Newspapers: “CalEnviroScreen, developed by the California Office of Environmental Health Hazard Assessment, is an interactive pollution tracking map that combines environmental, health and socioeconomic data sets to show which communities experience the greatest cumulative environmental burdens. The latest update, CalEnviroScreen 5.0, is now available in draft form for public comment before the final version is released later this year.”

item.title: Recordly: Free Open-Source Screen Recorder with Auto-Zoom
item.description: Abduzeedo: “Most screen recording tools dump raw footage and leave the rest to you. Recordly, an open-source screen recorder built by developer webadderall, takes a different approach. It handles the visual polish automatically, so the gap between recording and shipping is much smaller.”

item.title: PwC will say goodbye to staff who aren’t convinced about AI
item.description: The Register: “You’ll use AI and like it too – if you work for PwC. Paul Griggs, US chief executive of the global professional services giant, has made clear there is no room at the corporation for AI skeptics.”

item.title: Seoul Museums Unveil K-Culture Programs for BTS
item.description: The Chosun Daily: “Museums, art galleries, and libraries are presenting a rich array of ‘K-Culture Programs’ in line with the BTS comeback concert held at Gwanghwamun, Seoul. The Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism announced on the 19th, ‘To allow global visitors to Korea to deeply experience Korean culture, special programs will be operated at five major national cultural institutions from the 20th.'”

item.title: Indiana law opens door for cryptocurrency in public retirement plans
item.description: Indianapolis Recorder: “Gov. Mike Braun signed House Bill 1042 (HB 1042) on March 3. The law allows public retirement plans to offer cryptocurrency investment options and seeks to standardize digital asset regulations across the state.”

item.title: Competition watchdog cracks knuckles, probes legality of Adobe cancellation fee
item.description: The Register: “Britain’s competition watchdog is opening an investigation into Adobe’s early cancellation fees on membership plans to ascertain if it breaks consumer law.”

item.title: A wave of posts claimed Benjamin Netanyahu was dead. Here’s how it spread.
item.description: Poynter: “Rumors of Netanyahu’s death were fueled by both real news and out-of-context videos, fake images and accusations that the Israeli government was using artificial intelligence to deceive the public about Netanyahu’s health and whereabouts.”

item.title: How sewage treatment plants could handle food waste, sparing landfills and the climate
item.description: The Conversation: “When we compared greenhouse gas emissions for the same food waste composition, we found that sending food to a landfill would emit 58.2 kilograms (129 pounds) of carbon dioxide equivalent per ton of food waste. In comparison, we looked at a conventional wastewater treatment plant, the type of plant most common in the U.S. It achieved net-negative emissions of –0.03 kilograms (about 1 ounce) of carbon dioxide equivalent per ton of food waste treated.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: ‘Mister Rogers’ Neighborhood’ Getting YouTube Channel For First Time
item.description: Deadline: “As part of the agreement, All3Media-owned Little Dot’s team in the U.S. will work with Fred Rogers Productions to launch and manage the channel, providing strategic insight, content curation and paid media services. The channel will include full-length episodes and a collection of repurposed digital-first content, including clips, shorts and compilations.”

item.title: OpenAI is putting ChatGPT, its browser and code generator into one desktop app
item.description: Engadget: “OpenAI is developing a ‘super app’ for desktop that unifies ChatGPT, its browser and its Codex app, according to the Wall Street Journal and CNBC. A company spokesperson told the publications that OpenAI Chief of Applications Fidji Simo will lead the application revamp with assistance from OpenAI President Greg Brockman.”

item.title: Russia Scales Up Disinformation Operations with AI, New Report Shows
item.description: United24: “Russia is increasing the scale of its disinformation operations with artificial intelligence, according to the Center for Countering Disinformation on March 20. The agency, citing the European External Action Service’s (EEAS) latest threat assessment, reported that 540 cases of foreign information manipulation and interference were recorded in 2025.”

item.title: These 6 simple tricks will turn your Android phone into an eReader
item.description: How-To Geek: “Unless you’ve got a phone with an e-ink display, you won’t be able to get a one-to-one eReader experience on a phone. That said, with a few tweaks, you can get pretty close. The tricks shared below can be especially handy if you’ve got an old phone or tablet lying around that you’d like to turn into an Android-based eReader.”

item.title: Bachelor Nation, #MomTok furious over violent video of Taylor Frankie Paul
item.description: Mashable: “Paul is a #MomTok influencer, with over 6 million followers, and the star of Hulu’s reality hit, The Secret Lives of Mormon Wives…. The 2023 video, released by TMZ, shows Paul kicking Mortensen and putting him in a chokehold while Paul’s young daughter is nearby on a couch. Paul then starts throwing metal chairs at Mortensen. One chair appears to graze the child, who begins crying.”

item.title: OpenAI is acquiring open source Python tool-maker Astral
item.description: Ars Technica: “OpenAI announced Thursday that it has entered into an agreement to acquire Astral, the company behind popular open source Python development tools such as uv, Ruff, and ty, and integrate the company into its Codex team.”

item.title: After this game dev shared her prototype online, it took less than 5 hours for someone to post their vibecoded knockoff
item.description: PC Gamer: “Shameless videogame knockoffs are a tale as old as time, of course; once something crosses a critical threshold of attention, it’s inevitable that clones will flood the iOS app store soon afterwards in a mad rush to capitalize on the zeitgeist. … But [Freya] Holmér told PC Gamer that AI coding tools are accelerating the rate at which imitators can cash in on someone else’s creativity.”

item.title: Concerns Over Meta’s Smart Glasses Have Reached the U.S. Senate
item.description: Gizmodo: “Consternation about smart glasses is ramping up, and it looks like those fears are officially hitting the national stage. This week, U.S. Sens. Ron Wyden and Jeff Merkley (both D-Ore) officially inquired about Meta’s plans to add facial recognition to its Ray-Ban smart glasses, painting the idea as an existential threat to privacy.”

item.title: Brazil rolls out law boosting online protection of minors
item.description: ABC News: “A Brazilian law that seeks to shield minors from addictive, violent and pornographic online content took effect this week, with experts calling it a milestone in the protection of children and adolescents.”

item.title: human.json
item.description: Spotted in my RSS feeds: “human.json is a lightweight protocol for humans to assert authorship of their site content and vouch for the humanity of others. It uses URL ownership as identity, and trust propagates through a crawlable web of vouches between sites.”

item.title: Removing Government Notices from Newspapers Reduces Citizen Participation in Decision-Making
item.description: Yale University: “In some states, lawmakers want to eliminate a centuries-old requirement to publish public notices about local government actions in newspapers. A study of Florida co-authored by Yale SOM’s Anya Nakhmurina found that weakening this rule appeared to decrease residents’ engagement and may have allowed unpopular decisions to proceed under the radar.”

item.title: San Jose thrift shop turns vintage finds into funding for historic preservation efforts
item.description: Local News Matters Bay Area: “Housed in a 5,000-square-foot warehouse, the Found SJ Rummage & Reuse Hub provides a second life for items while supporting the efforts of the Preservation Action Council of San Jose. The nonprofit works to safeguard San Jose’s cultural heritage and unique buildings, and releases an annual ‘Endangered Eight’ list of spaces threatened by neglect and development. The thrift shop is open Saturdays from 11 a.m. to 6 p.m.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New “Creating Pride in Families” Resource for Working Parents and Caregivers Launches
item.description: PFLAG: “With more than 50 years of experience supporting parents, families, and non-family allies of LGBTQ+ people, PFLAG National has pulled together best practices, resources, and tools to help companies launch, maintain, and revitalize internal peer-support groups for employees.”

item.title: Fortnite will return to Google’s Play Store globally on March 19
item.description: Engadget: “The game will return to the Play Store globally on March 19, the same day that the next Fortnite season goes live. It previously dropped back onto the Play Store in the US in December.”

item.title: WordPress.com now lets AI agents write and publish posts, and more
item.description: TechCrunch: “Web hosting platform WordPress.com is embracing AI agents, a decision that could change the look and feel of the web. The company announced Friday that it will now allow AI agents to draft, edit, and publish content on customers’ websites, as well as manage comments, update and fix metadata, organize content with tags and categories.”

item.title: YouTube killed my comment alerts, so I vibe-coded a fix to get them back – in just 1 hour
item.description: ZDNet: “As I walk you through how I did this task, please keep in mind how you can AI a solution out of almost anything. It’s not that I expect many of you will need email-based notifications for YouTube comments. But most of you reading this will want to create something to solve a problem that you alone want to solve.”

item.title: PewDiePie was sick of suffering from “algo brain,” so he “fixed YouTube”
item.description: Tubefilter: “The creator who was once the biggest thing on YouTube is now in his mad scientist era, and his tinkering has allowed him to develop a tool that takes the mental taxation out of social media scrolling. PewDiePie‘s browser extension, which he built using his personal AI model, takes users straight to their Subscriptions page when they log into their YouTube accounts.”

item.title: Naver to offer special map service tailored to BTS comeback concert
item.description: Yonhap News Agency: “South Korea’s top search engine operator Naver Corp. said Friday it will offer a special map service tailored to this week’s comeback concert by K-pop sensation BTS, helping fans locate information desks and other facilities at the venue.”

item.title: Judge Says Witness Wore Smart Glasses to Sneakily Inform Their Testimony
item.description: Gizmodo: “In a ruling published online earlier this month, and first reported by Legal Futures, [Judge Raquel] Agnello said [Laimonas] Jakstys had been wearing smart glasses connected to his phone and was being coached on his responses while testifying.”

item.title: KY social media lawsuit trust fund would provide resources for kids
item.description: Forward Kentucky: “Proposed Kentucky legislation would create a state trust fund for positive youth development programming using future settlement funds from social media company lawsuits.”

item.title: For AI Help, More College Students Ask Social Media First
item.description: Inside Higher Ed: “The most common education-related use for the technology in 2025 was completing assignments more efficiently (44 percent), followed by enhancing learning and understanding (38 percent), exploring additional learning resources (36 percent), and gaining access to AI-driven tutoring or assistance (35 percent). In 2024, enhancing learning and understanding was the most common use, cited by 45 percent of respondents.”

item.title: Moogle Gaps serves up misdirections instead of shortest routes — and that’s the point
item.description: TrendWatching: “Whipped up by two Australian ex-Droga5 creatives, Paul Meates and Henry Kimber, Moogle Gaps is an anti-wayfinder. Users input their navigational query as they normally would, but instead of the most efficient route from A to B, the app offers misdirections — or as its builders put it, ‘a way to get lost, visit a bar that‘s not local, or go to a restaurant where no one knows you.'” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Pick Tennessee Products Unveils New Website to Better Connect Consumers with Local Producers
item.description: Tennessee Department of Agriculture: “The website redesign follows continued growth in the Pick Tennessee Products program, which includes nearly 3,200 active members. The updated site focuses on improving the user experience and strengthening connections between Tennessee consumers and local Tennessee producers.”

item.title: Elon Musk misled Twitter investors ahead of $44 billion acquisition, jury says
item.description: CNBC: “A jury in California found that Elon Musk defrauded Twitter shareholders during the runup to his $44 billion acquisition of the social media company, according to a verdict issued on Friday. Total damages could reach up to $2.6 billion, attorneys for the plaintiffs said.”

item.title: Jurors wade through daunting evidence in high-stakes Meta trial about social media risks to children
item.description: Associated Press: “A daunting stream of testimony and evidence has been presented in a New Mexico case that explores what the social media conglomerate Meta knew about the effects of its platforms on children.”

item.title: Finding Your Most Popular Bluesky Followers
item.description: Raymond Camden: “A long time, like, a really long time ago, I created a web app that would take your Twitter followers and then sort them by the number of followers they had. … We all know what happened to the Twitter API, and Twitter itself, but last night I decided to take a stab at building something similar for Bluesky.”

item.title: Thousands have swooned over this MAGA dream girl. She’s made with AI.
item.description: Washington Post: This link goes to a MSN-syndicated version of the article (no paywall). “[Jessica] Foster’s viral takeoff highlights an increasingly prevalent strategy for winning online attention. A slew of right-wing accounts, peddling patriotism mixed with soft-core pornography, use fake women and convincing imagery to grab viewers across a distracted internet, monetize their interest and score political points.”

item.title: CBS News to Shutter Its Storied Radio Division
item.description: Radio World: “CBS News will shut down CBS News Radio on May 22 as part of a restructuring that includes a 6% reduction in staff. The development will leave approximately 700 affiliated stations seeking another source for features such as news at the top of the hour.”

item.title: Pinterest CEO calls on governments to ban social media for users under 16
item.description: TechCrunch: “Pinterest’s CEO, Bill Ready, has called for governments to ban social media for users under 16 in a new Time op-ed.”

item.title: Cyber actors linked to Russia targeting users of messaging apps, FBI says
item.description: Reuters: “Hackers tied to the Russian intelligence services are targeting users of consumer ‌messaging applications such as Signal, the FBI ‌and U.S. cyber defense agency CISA said on Friday.”

item.title: Japan to allow ‘proactive cyber-defense’ from October 1st
item.description: The Register: “Japan’s government yesterday decided to allow its Self-Defense Force to conduct offensive cyber-operations, starting on October 1st.”

item.title: Apple can delist apps “with or without cause,” judge says in loss for Musi app
item.description: Ars Technica: “Musi, a free music-streaming app that had tens of millions of iPhone downloads and garnered plenty of controversy over its method of acquiring music, has lost an attempt to get back on Apple’s App Store. A federal judge dismissed Musi’s lawsuit against Apple with prejudice and sanctioned Musi’s lawyers for ‘mak[ing] up facts to fill the perceived gaps in Musi’s case.'”

item.title: ChatGPT vs. DeepSeek: What 5,000 Chinese Stocks Reveal About AI’s Limits
item.description: Harvard Business Review: “ChatGPT, owned by US-based OpenAI, issued far rosier forecasts—with higher price targets and more ‘buy’ recommendations—than its Chinese rival DeepSeek when each platform evaluated nearly 5,000 publicly traded Chinese companies, says research by Harvard Business School’s Charles C.Y. Wang. This surprising result is attributed to disparities in information availability: ChatGPT appears to incorporate less coverage from Chinese media.”

item.title: Using AI makes writing more bland, study finds
item.description: NBC News: “The research team found that users who heavily relied on large language models (LLMs) produced responses that diverged significantly in meaning from the answers of participants who only partially relied on LLMs or avoided their use altogether, suggesting heavy AI use alters the substance of humans’ arguments in addition to changing writing style.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: The Broad Center at Yale SOM Launches Repository of Data on School System Leaders
item.description: Yale School of Management: “Publicly available through the data management platform GitHub, the repository currently includes a dataset of superintendents in more than 10,000 of the approximately 13,000 public school districts in the U.S., comprising over 180,000 data points across 23 states and covering a majority of public school enrollment from 2010 to 2022.”

item.title: OpenAI’s GPT-5.4 mini and nano launch – with near flagship performance at much lower cost
item.description: ZDNet: “The latest GPT-5.4 mini model delivers benchmark results surprisingly close to the full GPT-5.4 model while running much faster, signaling a shift toward smaller AI models powering real-world applications.”

item.title: Kagi Translate’s AI answers the question “What would horny Margaret Thatcher say?”
item.description: Ars Technica: “This week, many people across the Internet have been bemused to find that the AI-powered Kagi Translate can perform these and countless other unlikely ‘translation’ tasks. And while the collective discovery highlights the playful, creative side of large language models, it also exposes the risks of letting users play with generalized LLM tools.”

item.title: A new hybrid model is coming to the VTuber world. Say hello to the “XTuber.”
item.description: Tubefilter: “Before we go any further, let’s clear a few things up: XTubers are not tied to the platform formerly known as Twitter, nor are they delivering adult content. In this case, the X represents the word ‘cross,’ and the full term refers to the idea that the typical XTuber is a crossover between a VTuber and a traditional creator.”

item.title: A number of US cities are pulling the plug on Flock Safety’s AI cameras
item.description: TechSpot: “A growing number of US cities are ending contracts with Flock Safety, the Atlanta-based company whose AI-powered camera systems have rapidly proliferated across the country. Originally promoted as a public safety tool, the company’s technology is now at the center of a broader national debate over the use of artificial intelligence in law enforcement and immigration enforcement.”

item.title: Tech companies are teaming up to combat scammers
item.description: Engadget: “As first reported by Axios, Google, Microsoft, LinkedIn, Meta, Amazon, OpenAI, Adobe, Levi Strauss & Co, Target, Pinterest and Match Group announced the signing of the Industry Accord Against Online Scams and Fraud. The new agreement is meant to put up a united industry-wide front against online fraud and scams, particularly those from sophisticated criminal networks that use multiple platforms.”

item.title: Using AI to verify human advice could damage your professional relationships
item.description: PsyPost: “New research published in Computers in Human Behavior suggests that consulting artificial intelligence (AI) for advice may unintentionally strain relationships with human professionals.”

item.title: Study: Teen girls are using AI to create sexual imagery
item.description: Mashable: “A new study suggests that teen girls use so-called nudification apps at the same rate as teen boys. The artificial intelligence-powered undressing tools allow users to create sexualized images of a person, typically by uploading a picture of them. The results surprised Dr. Chad M.S. Steel, a digital forensics researcher at George Mason University who studies technology-facilitated crimes against children.”

item.title: AI Creep Is Real
item.description: Mike Kentz: “A year ago, I had one ChatGPT window open and I was giving it my full attention. I remember hearing about people who ran multiple custom bots simultaneously — rotating through them, orchestrating conversations between agents — and thinking they were out of their minds. Eight months later I had three Claude Projects open at once.”

item.title: New Mobile App Turns Phones into At-Home Fetal Heart Monitors
item.description: Georgia Tech: “Studies show that one in five pregnant women experiences perinatal anxiety, which is characterized by intense negative thoughts about their pregnancy. DopFone turns any smartphone speaker into a Doppler radar by emitting a low-pitched ultrasound and detecting reflected signals of abdominal surface vibrations caused by a fetal heartbeat.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: The Masters Outdoes Itself Again, Unveils New ‘Vault’ Built For The Golf Sickos Out There
item.description: OutKick: “There certainly isn’t a lack of Masters content readily available to the public, and three weeks out from the 2026 edition of the event, a new feature built for the true golf sickos out there has been unveiled called the ‘Masters Vault.’ The vault is a video archive where users can search and watch any shot of every single final round, dating all the way back to 1968.”

item.title: New York City to host 10th annual Open Data Week
item.description: StateScoop: “The event, which originally launched as part the city’s 2012 Open Data law, will feature more than 80 free or low-cost in-person and virtual programs, including a new documentary film festival, a data art exhibition, a two-day conference and daily classes teaching residents how to make use of the city’s 6.3 billion rows of data.”

item.title: National survey of NIH-funded researchers shows precarious state of U.S. science — ‘This is like the Titanic’
item.description: STAT News: “Strikingly, despite courts reversing some grant terminations and Congress thwarting plans to slash the NIH budget, just 35% of respondents whose grants were cut or delayed said their government funding had been fully restored by the end of 2025.”

item.title: ‘The model no longer works:’ Crypto landlord’s Detroit enterprise is crumbling
item.description: Outlier Media: “RealT, a cryptocurrency real estate company that owns hundreds of rental homes in Detroit, appears to be unraveling. The company has stopped almost all weekly payouts to investors. It owes millions of dollars in unpaid property taxes, water bills and blight tickets. And it faces the possibility that more than 300 Detroit properties could be pushed into tax foreclosure by the end of March.”

item.title: Iran’s ‘chosen users’ get ‘privileged access’ despite internet blackout for masses
item.description: The Register: “Alp Toker, director at NetBlocks, told The Register that some users can, in theory, gain access to the web, but only through channels not under state control, which are few and highly expensive. They are not available to the average person.”

item.title: Millions of iPhones can be hacked with a new tool found in the wild
item.description: Ars Technica: “Researchers at Google and cybersecurity firms iVerify and Lookout on Wednesday jointly revealed the discovery of a sophisticated iPhone hacking technique known as DarkSword that they’ve seen in use on infected websites, capable of instantly and silently hacking iOS devices that visit those sites.”

item.title: Streaming fraud man who pocketed $8m using hundreds of thousands of AI songs streamed billions of times by bots pleads guilty
item.description: Music Business Worldwide: “The man at the center of what’s been described as the first-ever criminal prosecution for AI-assisted streaming fraud in the United States has pleaded guilty. Michael Smith, of Cornelius, North Carolina, pleaded guilty today (March 19) to one count of conspiracy to commit wire fraud before U.S. District Judge John G. Koeltl in the Southern District of New York.”

item.title: BMG Sues Anthropic, Entering AI Copyright Battlefield: ‘Egregious Law-Breaking’
item.description: Billboard: “The various publishing arms of BMG filed a lawsuit on Tuesday (March 17) against the behemoth company, which is behind the popular AI chatbot Claude. BMG alleges the model was trained on lyrics from unlicensed songs, including Billboard Hot 100 chart-toppers like Ariana Grande’s ‘7 Rings’ and Bruno Mars’ ‘Uptown Funk,’ and now spits out infringing lyrics when prompted.”

item.title: How Edvard Munch’s painting The Scream might look in 300 years’ time
item.description: Norweigan SciTech News: “Edvard Munch used materials that make his paintings vulnerable to the ravages of time. A new digital tool now shows how much The Scream may change over the next 300 years.”

item.title: Top AI coding tools make mistakes one in four times
item.description: University of Waterloo: “Even the most advanced models achieved only about 75 per cent accuracy in the tests, while open-source models performed closer to 65 per cent. The study evaluated 11 LLM models across 18 structured output formats and 44 tasks designed to assess how reliably the systems followed structured rules.”

item.title: Popular AI chatbots generate unsafe diet plans for teenagers
item.description: PsyPost: “Many teenagers trying to manage their weight are turning to artificial intelligence chatbots to generate personalized diet plans. However, a new study published in Frontiers in Nutrition reveals that these computer-generated menus often fall short on basic calories and fail to provide the proper balance of essential nutrients. Following these flawed digital recommendations could put young people at risk of nutritional deficiencies during a period of rapid physical growth.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Yahoo Hong Kong to begin ‘phased wind-down’ of news business in April
item.description: Hong Kong Free Press: “Yahoo Hong Kong’s pivot to original content in 2021 allowed the company to fill a gap left behind by independent outlets Apple Daily and Stand News, which shut down that year in the wake of the Beijing-imposed national security law.”

item.title: YouTube tests sticky banner after ad skip
item.description: Search Engine Land: “YouTube is testing a sticky banner overlay that appears once a user skips an ad. Instead of the ad disappearing entirely, a branded card remains on-screen until the viewer actively dismisses it.”

item.title: I switched to a local LLM for these 5 tasks and the cloud version hasn’t been worth it since
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Local LLMs have also come a long way, to the point where you can run lightweight AI models on just about every device. They’re not good at everything, but they do some tasks so well you’d want to cancel that cloud AI subscription right away.”

item.title: ChatGPT’s sex-centered adult mode raises red flags at OpenAI
item.description: Mashable: ” The company’s well being advisory council said in a January meeting that they were in unanimous agreement that the company should not move forward with the proposed adult mode, insiders told WSJ. Concerns from psychologists and cognitive scientists had gone ignored, they said, after warning that X-rated chats could foster unhealthy emotional dependence — an existing problem with standard ChatGPT users.”

item.title: Beyond the Feed: A Flickr friendship that became an exhibition
item.description: Flickr Blog: “As a community built for photographers, we love celebrating the connections Flickr helps spark, whether friendships, collaborations, mentorships or any other bonds formed through a shared love of photography. That’s exactly what drew us to the story of Christopher Evans and Juliette Melia, whose Flickr connection many years ago blossomed into real life collaboration – a gallery exhibition featuring Christopher’s work which opened this past week.”

item.title: Museums looted of priceless artifacts as Sudan counts the cost of a deadly conflict
item.description: NBC News: “The preliminary losses across the culture, antiquities and tourism sector during the war stand at $110 million, according to an estimate from Sudan’s minister of culture and information, Khalid Ali Aleisir, who said that figure captures only part of the irreversible damage inflicted on repositories of African history.”

item.title: Ford campaign warns crypto funded PAC to cease and desist ‘defamatory’ ads
item.description: Forest Park Review: “A lawyer for 7th Congressional candidate La Shawn K. Ford sent a cease-and-desist order to a crypto currency funded PAC March 10, demanding it stop producing and disseminating video and print political attack ads containing what it calls ‘false, misleading, and defamatory statements’ against Ford.”

item.title: AI Tools Like ChatGPT Make Learning Easier — and More Persuasive, Yale Study Finds
item.description: Yale University: “With funding from ISPS, [Professor Daniel] Karell and his team set out to find if reading AI-written summaries of history help people learn better than reading human-written ones…. In a paper published in December in Social Science Computer Review, the researchers found that people who read AI-written summaries answered more questions correctly than those who read human-written ones.”

item.title: Artificial intelligence struggles to consistently evaluate scientific facts
item.description: PsyPost: “A recent study shows that when an artificial intelligence is asked the exact same question multiple times, it often gives completely different answers. These results, published in the Rutgers Business Review, highlight the limits of current automated reasoning and the ongoing need for human oversight.”

item.title: Utopia Tokyo: Interactive Web Design Meets Japanese Masks
item.description: abduzeedo: “The core of the site is a collection of 14 Japanese masks — Samurai, Oni, Hannya, Tengu, Kitsune, Kappa, Noh, Kendo, and more. Each mask is rendered as a highly detailed 3D object. They appear in a grid layout with animated frame corners that pulse like targeting reticles. Clicking a mask opens a detail panel with cultural context: the Samurai mask, for instance, is described as worn in battle to intimidate foes and reflect a warrior spirit.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: US archive makes millions of NSDAP files available online
item.description: Blue News: “In contrast to Germany, the USA provides access to a complete digital copy of the microfilmed NSDAP Central Index and NSDAP Local Group Index. This means that more than 16 million digital objects such as photos on more than 5000 digitized microfilm rolls are now freely available. These contain the data of millions of Germans who were members of the National Socialist German Workers’ Party (NSDAP) until 1945.”

item.title: Checkoff Launches Online Database To Help Farmers Find Grant Opportunities
item.description: Market Talk: “The dairy checkoff’s new online tool is designed to help dairy farmers and their advisors more easily identify grants and funding opportunities for conservation and on-farm improvements. The Funding Opportunities Database, available through the Dairy Conservation Navigator, organizes federal, state and private funding programs into a single searchable platform tailored to dairy operations.”

item.title: Exclusive: Small publishers hit hardest by search traffic declines
item.description: Axios: “Over the past two years, referral traffic from traditional search engines has declined by 60% for small publishers, compared with 47% for medium-sized publishers and 22% for large publishers, per Chartbeat.”

item.title: YouTube is outsourcing its AI slop problem to you, and that’s a terrible idea
item.description: DigitalTrends: “YouTube has a new plan to deal with the wave of AI-generated content flooding its platform, and it involves you. The company is now asking viewers to rate whether a video feels like AI slop. On the surface, that sounds like a reasonable way to tackle low-quality AI content in your feed. In practice, it may cause more problems than it solves.”

item.title: Google is making microdramas
item.description: Tubefilter: “Per Business Insider, one of the ultimate goals with 100 Zeros is to get more creatives using Google’s tech products (including its increasingly dogged push into generative AI), and get more young people thinking those same products are #cool. Riding that coolness wave, 100 Zeros’ latest project is a slate of microdramas with big talent attached.”

item.title: Ad for AI editing app which said it could ‘remove anything’ banned
item.description: BBC: “The YouTube ad for PixVideo – AI Video Maker, seen in January, showed a ‘before’ and ‘after’ image of a young woman, with red scribble overlaid on her midriff in the former, and parts of her bare skin exposed in the latter. Text across the bottom of the picture stated: “Erase anything” followed by a heart-eyes emoji.”

item.title: North Korea’s 100,000-strong fake IT worker army rake in $500M a year for Kim Jong Un
item.description: The Register: “Researchers at IBM X‑Force and Flare Research have uncovered data that sheds light on how North Korea’s fake IT worker schemes operate and infiltrate companies in order to funnel money back to the regime and steal sensitive information.”

item.title: Saline County sheriff hopeful sues over lurid Facebook accusations
item.description: Arkansas Times: “Richard Friend, who is the chief of police in England, is in a runoff for the Saline County sheriff’s position. He filed suit on March 10 in Saline County Circuit Court against Kevin Cooper, Rick Cross and ‘John Does 1-5,’ saying they falsely accused him of corruption, theft and abuse of authority, among other crimes, and that the two men made the social media posts just prior to the start of early voting in the March 3 preferential primary to try to defeat him.”

item.title: Self-Host & Tech Independence: The Joy of Building Your Own
item.description: Simon Späti: “As I said, sharing what you work on, for everyone to see, will only benefit others to learn, but even more so you. As you get potential contributions or other forks that build something else on top of it. You get feedback and connecting with like-minded people. If nothing else, this is probably the most rewarding part of open-source. That you meet new people that you would have never met otherwise.”

item.title: “Eat the rich”? Dutch political parties slay on social media
item.description: Dutch News: “While some researchers are concerned about polarisation among young people and the huge reach of far-right parties such as Forum voor Democratie, Christians, Socialists and green advocates are taking them on.”

item.title: Narcissistic traits and celebrity worship are linked to excessive Instagram scrolling via emotional struggles and fear of missing out
item.description: PsyPost: “The researchers found a positive link between narcissistic traits, celebrity worship, and problematic Instagram use. In other words, individuals who scored higher in narcissism or celebrity obsession also reported unhealthier relationships with the app. However, the connection was not just a direct line from personality to addiction.”

item.title: Zip-Drive Emulator Puts Big Disks Back On LPT
item.description: Hackaday: “[Minh Danh] is one of those who still has affection for Zip drives, and when his parallel port Zip 100 drive started to give up the ghost last year, he decided to do something bold: reverse engineer it, and produce an emulator. First software, and then in hardware.” Good morning, Internet…
